relevance_reason: Identifies an intronic ATTTC repeat expansion in STARD7 as the cause of FAME2 and shows it segregating with disease in 22 families.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized the clinical features of 22 FAME families. The families were mainly Italian; others were Australian/New Zealand, Sephardic Jewish (Iraqi and Israeli), South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian. Patients had cortical myoclonic tremor and myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset usually in the second to third decade. Expressivity varied within and between families, and the frequency of GTCS ranged from 15% to 100% across families. Some families also had focal seizures.
quotes: FAME (also referred to as Familial Cortical Myoclonic Tremor and Epilepsy or Benign Adult onset Familial Myoclonic Epilepsy [OMIM phenotypic series: PS601068]) is characterised by cortical myoclonic tremor and overt myoclonic and later generalised tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS).

Onset of symptoms occurs in the second to third decade with variable expressivity within and between families; anticipation has been noted in some families. The frequency of GTCS varies from 15 to 100% in 22 different families reported here (Table 1).
findings.population: Australian/New Zealand, Italian, Sephardic Jewish, South African, French, Spanish, Syrian

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) described a large Australian/New Zealand family of European ancestry (Family 1) with 55 affected members. All 55 had myoclonus/cortical tremor, 8 (15%) had tonic-clonic seizures, and 2 (4%) had focal seizures. Mean age of onset was 18.6 years, with a range of 4 to 60 years.
quotes: 1 | Australian/New Zealand of European ancestry | 55 | 18.6 y [4–59,60 y] | 55/55 (100%) | 8/55 (15%) | 2/55 (4%) |

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) found evidence of anticipation in the large Australian/New Zealand FAME2 family. Median age of onset was 30 years in generation III (n = 6), 17 years in generation IV (n = 30), and 12 years in generation V (n = 16).
quotes: We found evidence of anticipation; generation III had a median onset of 30 years (range 14–60 y, n = 6), in generation IV median onset was 17 years (8–50 y, n = 30) and the median onset in generation V was 12 years (4–19 y, n = 16).

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) analysed whole-genome sequencing data from affected members of 3 FAME families (Families 1, 3 and 19) using ExpansionHunter and exSTRa. In all FAME samples tested, they found an expansion of an ATTTT repeat together with an inserted ATTTC repeat within the first intron of STARD7. The ATTTC repeat was absent from WGS data on 69 controls.
quotes: This revealed an expansion of an ATTTT repeat and insertion of an ATTTC repeat in the context of the reverse strand of chr2 within the first intron of STARD7 (StAR-related lipid transfer domain-containing 7) in all FAME samples tested (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1).

The ATTTC repeat was not present in any whole-genome sequencing data from 69 control samples (Supplementary Fig. 1), nor is it reported in the Simple Repeats track in the UCSC genome browser (build hg38).

variants.as_reported: intronic ATTTC repeat insertion/expansion with expanded ATTTT repeat

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) used a repeat-primed PCR assay and detected the STARD7 ATTTC expansion in all 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families. It was also present in all 20 affected individuals from 6 additional multiplex families and in 1 of 52 unrelated singleton cases, giving 158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 families. Two individuals without a FAME diagnosis carried the expansion and were likely presymptomatic, and 8 of 13 individuals with an uncertain diagnosis were carriers. The expansion was not found in 28 controls.
quotes: We developed a repeat-primed PCR (RP-PCR) assay to rapidly identify the expansion in 137/137 affected individuals from 16 independently reported FAME2 families worldwide
Of these, 20/20 familial and 1/52 singleton cases were positive for an ATTTC expansion in STARD7
The ATTTC expansions segregate in 158/158 individuals typically affected by FAME from 22 pedigrees including 16 previously reported families recruited worldwide.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) used long-read sequencing to show the repeat structure. In one patient from Family 1, a SMRT read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats, while a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats; the authors suggested this reflected somatic variation. A patient from Family 5 had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, 4645 bp in total. The repeat structure on the forward strand was (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n.
quotes: The SMRT read generated to 99% base accuracy by circular consensus calling was comprised of four subreads and contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats, without interruption from other sequences.
The Oxford Nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions, suggesting somatic variation of repeat sizes may occur within the one individual.
a single Oxford Nanopore read spanned the expanded repeats with 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats; 4645 bp in total length.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) found the STARD7 ATTTC expansion in 2 families (Families 4 and 15) that carried the previously reported ADRA2B variant c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG. The authors stated that this strongly suggested the ADRA2B allele is not causative.
quotes: This included two families with the previously identified ADRA2B; c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.H225_L229delinsQ225_F_G_R228 variant strongly suggesting that allele is not causative (Table 1; Family 4 & 15).

findings.statement: In patient-derived fibroblasts, Corbett et al. (2019) found that STARD7 mRNA levels (by qPCR and RNA-seq) and protein levels (by Western blot) were not altered. RNA-seq detected no reads containing ATTTC repeats. The authors suggested that the repeat sequence itself is pathogenic, independent of any effect on the encompassing gene.
quotes: RNA-Seq data from six patient-derived fibroblasts (four from Family 1 and two from Family 5) showed there was no significant difference in gene expression of STARD7 between affected and unaffected individuals along the entire length of the gene
Reads containing ATTTC repeats were not present in the RNA-Seq data despite robust expression of STARD7.
These data suggest the repeat sequence alone is pathogenic, independent of an effect on the coding sequence of the encompassing gene.

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) stated that the FAME2 locus is the most frequently linked region in Caucasian individuals with FAME. By contrast, chromosome 8 linkage has so far been limited to Asian individuals.
quotes: The FAME2 locus is the most frequently observed linked region for Caucasian individuals affected by this disorder whereas chromosome 8 thus far is limited to Asian individuals

findings.statement: Corbett et al. (2019) found that the ATTTC repeat primer was diagnostic for FAME, with 100% sensitivity in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chromosome 2. The endogenous ATTTT repeat varied in length naturally and was not suitable for screening.
quotes: The natural variability in the length of the endogenous ATTTT repeat sequence meant that is was not feasible to use that sequence for mutation screening; however, the ATTTC repeat primer was diagnostic for FAME with a sensitivity of 100% in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chr2.

relevance_reason: The paper identifies the ADRA2B in-frame indel as the cause of ADCME/FAME2 in two Italian families. It also describes the patients' clinical features and reports functional studies.

findings.statement: De Fusco et al. (2014) described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) as a familial disorder with cortical reflex myoclonus. It shows as action-induced shivering movements of the hands and jerking of the upper limbs, variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures of variable severity. A minority of patients have borderline or moderately impaired cognition, and myoclonus often worsens in advanced age.
quotes: ADCME is characterized by familial occurrence of cortical reflex myoclonus manifested as action-induced shivering movement of the hands and upper limb jerking variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures of variable severity and, in a minority of patients, with borderline or moderately impaired cognitive skills.
Worsening of myoclonus is often observed in advanced age.

findings.statement: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a 4-generation Tuscan family (family B) with 5 affected members. All had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs, and cortical tremor was the presenting symptom, starting between ages 18 and 50 years. All but one (IV:1) had epilepsy with rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures, at times triggered by visual stimuli; 2 patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognitive level and the others had normal intelligence. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflex studies were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. Brain MRI was normal where performed.
quotes: family B is a four-generation kindred including 5 affected members (4 living). All patients exhibited postural hand and upper limbs myoclonus.

Epilepsy occurred in all but one (IV:1) individuals and was characterized by rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures, at times precipitated by visual stimuli, occurring in all patients and by drug resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures occurring in patients III: 2 and III:5.
Cortical tremor was the presenting symptom in all affected individuals, appearing between the ages of 18 to 50 years.

phenotypes.text: postural hand and upper limb myoclonus
drug-resistant focal or complex partial seizures
generalized or focal paroxysmal EEG activity

findings.statement: De Fusco et al. (2014) found no cardiovascular disease on careful history in any of the ADCME patients. Two of the oldest ADRA2B mutation carriers developed age-related dementia.
quotes: A careful anamnesis was performed on all ADCME patients giving negative evidence for cardiovascular diseases; two of the oldest ADRA2B mutation carriers developed age-related dementia.

findings.statement: In a 5-generation Tuscan family (family A) with ADCME previously mapped to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, De Fusco et al. (2014) used candidate gene sequencing to identify a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.H225_L229delinsQFGR). The change replaces 5 amino acids (HGGAL) in the third intracellular loop with 4 new residues (QFGR). The indel segregated completely with the disease and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls, dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and 1000 Genomes. Targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of the critical region in 2 affected members found it to be the only relevant change.
quotes: we identified a novel in-frame insertion/deletion in the α2-adrenergic receptor subtype B gene (α2B-AR; ADRA2B), which substitutes five amino acids, HGGAL, with four new residues, QFGR, (indel; c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.H225_L229delinsQ225_F_G_R228)
This indel mutation completely co-segregates with the disease phenotype and is absent in 575 unrelated controls from Tuscany
The ADRA2B mutation was confirmed as the unique relevant chance (data not shown).

findings.statement: De Fusco et al. (2014) found the same ADRA2B indel in a second Tuscan ADCME family (family B). Family histories showed no known kinship between the 2 families, but they shared the same disease haplotype across the entire chromosome 2 critical region, suggesting a common ancestor.
quotes: In a second ADCME family from Tuscany (Fig. 1; Family B) we detected the same indel of the ADRA2B gene.

Although no kinship between the two families was discovered by anamnestic analysis of members of the two pedigrees, a common ancestor is to be expected as they share the same disease haplotype spanning the entire critical region on chromosome 2

findings.statement: De Fusco et al. (2014) sequenced BAFME pedigrees from southern Italy that map to the ADCME locus and found no ADRA2B mutations; Southern blot excluded large insertions or deletions. The authors suggested that ADCME and BAFME/FAME may be classified as 2 distinct clinical entities, although they could not exclude variants in regulatory or noncoding regions.
quotes: BAFME pedigrees originating from Southern Italy have been shown to map in the ADCME locus. However, we failed to detect any ADRA2B mutations in these pedigrees by direct sequence analysis and excluded potential large insertion and deletions by southern blot
We did not detect any mutation in ADRA2B in BAFME/FAME patients, suggesting the possibility of classifying ADCME and BAFME/FAME as two distinct clinical entities.

findings.statement: De Fusco et al. (2014) found that the indel lies on the common ADRA2B allele with 12 consecutive glutamic acid residues, not on the less common polymorphic short allele that is associated with cardiovascular and metabolic risk.
quotes: However, the identified mutation is syntenic to the more common variant showing 12 consecutive glutamic acid residues, variant that is not associated to the above mentioned effects.

findings.statement: In transfected HeLa cells, De Fusco et al. (2014) showed that both wildtype and mutant ADRA2B localized normally to the plasma membrane. In the presence of arrestin-3, both moved to endosomes after epinephrine stimulation, indicating that the mutation did not impair protein maturation or arrestin-dependent internalization. Molecular modeling predicted that the mutation changes the conformation of the third intracellular loop.
quotes: Both wild type and mutant α2B-AR show the typical plasma membrane localization in the absence of agonist, indicating that the mutation does not affect the maturation of the protein in the ER-Golgi compartments and its delivery to the plasma membrane
These results suggest that both wild type and mutant α2B-AR internalize in an arrestin-3-dependent manner and that the arrestin-3 interaction with the 3i loop is not precluded by the mutation
the mutant is predicted to prominently alter the conformation of the specific region of the 3i loop.

findings.statement: In co-immunoisolation assays in CosM6 cells, De Fusco et al. (2014) found that spinophilin bound similar amounts of wildtype and mutant ADRA2B after 5 minutes of epinephrine. By 10 minutes, binding to the mutant had fallen back to basal levels while binding to wildtype stayed elevated, suggesting that the mutant cannot form a stable complex with spinophilin.
quotes: After 5-min treatment of epinephrine, spinophilin was co-immunoisolated with comparable amount of wild type and mutant α2B-AR. However, the amount of spinophilin co-isolated with the mutant α2B-AR dropped back to the basal level after epinephrine treatment for 10 min
These data suggest that the mutant α2B-AR cannot form a stable complex with spinophilin, which would result in lack of spinophilin regulation on responses mediated by this mutant α2B-AR.

findings.statement: In Xenopus oocytes, De Fusco et al. (2014) found that spinophilin significantly raised the EC50 for epinephrine-stimulated Ca(2+)-activated Cl- current with wildtype ADRA2B but not with the mutant receptor. They concluded that the mutant increases the intensity of Ca(2+) signaling. They proposed that the mutation has a gain-of-function effect by reducing the interaction with spinophilin, possibly leading to cortical hyperexcitability through impaired GABAergic inhibition.
quotes: The dose-response measurement showed that spinophilin significantly increased the EC50 for epinephrine (p<0.01; Fig.6)

but the presence of spinophilin does not result in an increase in EC50 (α2B-AR + SPN versus α2B-AR mutant + SPN: p<0.001; Fig.6). Therefore, we conclude that the mutant α2B-AR significantly increases the intensity of Ca2+ signaling by the receptors.
We propose that the ADCME mutation exerts a gain of function effect by reducing the interaction with spinophilin, and thus increasing receptor activity.

relevance_reason: Reports a large FAME family and narrows the FAME2 locus on chromosome 2.

findings.statement: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia, with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy. All 55 affected family members had fine hand tremor, usually beginning in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median age 17 years; range 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years).
quotes: A 6-generation FAME kindred of European descent was ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. Affected family members (N = 55) had fine hand tremor, with onset typically in adolescence (median age, 15 years; age range, 4-60 years).
Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%), arising later than hand tremor (median age, 17 years; age range, 5-60 years).
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (age range, 18-76 years).
findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

findings.statement: Crompton et al. (2012) found on neurophysiologic testing that affected members of the family had features of cortical reflex myoclonus. They concluded that the most common phenotype in this family was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, together with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus.
quotes: Neurophysiological testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus.
The most common FAME phenotype in this large family is mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are uncommon and occur around sleep onset following severe generalized myoclonus.
findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

findings.statement: In a 6-generation kindred with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy, Crompton et al. (2012) used genetic mapping to narrow the FAME2 locus on chromosome 2 to a 13.3-Mb interval containing 99 known protein-coding genes.
quotes: Genetic mapping narrows the FAME2 (OMIM 607876) locus on chromosome 2 to a 13.3-megabase interval, harboring 99 known protein-coding genes.
findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

findings.statement: Crompton et al. (2012) described familial adult myoclonic epilepsy as an autosomal dominant syndrome, and reported it in a 6-generation kindred.
quotes: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME) is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by a core triad of cortical tremor, multifocal myoclonus, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
findings.population: European descent; New Zealand and Australia

relevance_reason: Describes an Italian FCMTE family that shares a haplotype on chromosome 2 near the centromere, the FAME2 locus, after linkage to 8q24 was excluded.

findings.statement: Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected family members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested may be due to temporal lobe dysfunction.
quotes: Clinically affected members of the family had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus involving the eyelids during blinking.
Neuropsychological testing disclosed visuospatial impairment, possibly due to temporal lobe dysfunction.

findings.statement: In the Italian FCMTE family, Suppa et al. (2009) found neurophysiologic evidence suggesting increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.
quotes: Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased primary motor cortex excitability with normal sensorimotor integration.

findings.statement: In the Italian FCMTE family, Suppa et al. (2009) used linkage analysis to exclude the 8q24 locus. Affected members shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the region of chromosome 2 near the centromere.
quotes: Linkage analysis excluded the 8q24 locus, where patients shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the pericentromeric region of chromosome 2.

relevance_reason: Linkage and founder haplotype study placing BAFME in five Italian families at the chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 locus (FAME2).

findings.statement: Madia et al. (2008) genotyped 53 affected individuals from 5 southern Italian families with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME), one not previously reported, using microsatellite markers spanning chromosomes 2p11.1-q12.2 and 8q23.1-q24.11. Multipoint linkage analysis found significant linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, with a maximum cumulative lod score of 18.5 for markers D2S2161 and D2S388.
quotes: Five Italian BAFME families were identified. One family has not been previously reported. DNA from 53 affected individuals was genotyped with highly polymorphic microsatellite markers spanning chromosomes 2p11.1-q12.2 and 8q23.1-q24.11.
Significant linkage was found on chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 and a maximum cumulative lod score of 18.5 was found for markers D2S2161 and D2S388.

findings.statement: Madia et al. (2008) found that the haplotype '5332' of the adjacent markers D2S388, D2S2216, D2S113, and D2S2175 segregated with the disease in all 5 Italian BAFME families. They concluded that the same mutation, inherited from a common ancestor, segregates in these families, indicating a founder effect.
quotes: The haplotype "5332" of adjacent markers D2S388, D2S2216, D2S113, and D2S2175 segregates with the disease in all families indicating that the same mutation inherited from a common ancestor segregates in these families.

findings.statement: In a preliminary genotype-phenotype analysis, Madia et al. (2008) found only minor clinical differences among patients carrying the founder disease haplotype. They suggested that other factors do not markedly influence the expressivity of the founder mutation.
quotes: Preliminary genotype-phenotype showed that patients carrying the disease haplotype show minor clinical differences, suggesting that expressivity of the founder mutation is not markedly influenced by other factors.

findings.statement: Madia et al. (2008) described benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME or FAME) as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy.
quotes: Benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME or FAME) is an autosomal dominant condition, characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It reports refinement of the 2p11.1-q12.2 locus for cortical tremor with epilepsy (FAME2) and the exclusion of candidate genes, which is mapping evidence for this entry.

findings.statement: Saint-Martin et al. (2008) refined the 2p11.1-q12.2 locus responsible for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy and excluded candidate genes in the region.
quotes: Refinement of the 2p11.1-q12.2 locus responsible for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy and exclusion of candidate genes.

relevance_reason: Reports a large Italian family with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy linked to chromosome 2p, which is the FAME2 locus.

findings.statement: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members.
quotes: We report a five-generation family showing cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy, originating from Naples, Italy.
Eleven members, aged 24-56 years (mean: 39.2 years), suffered from hand tremor and myoclonus, whereas generalized seizures occurred in six.
Electrophysiological study confirmed the presence of cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members.

findings.statement: In the family studied by Striano et al. (2005), 3 presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I. After 1.5 years of follow-up, these members developed hand tremor and myoclonus of the upper limbs.
quotes: In addition, giant somatosensory-evoked potential components and enhanced long loop reflex I were found also in three presymptomatic members who manifested hand tremor and myoclonus at upper limbs after 1.5 years of follow-up.

findings.statement: By linkage analysis of an Italian family with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy, Striano et al. (2005) found significant linkage to chromosome 2p (maximum lod score of 5.9).
quotes: Genetic study of the pedigree revealed a significant linkage on chromosome 2p (maximum lod score = 5.9).

relevance_reason: Reports two Italian BAFME families linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, which is the FAME2 locus, and suggests allelism with ADCME.

findings.statement: de Falco et al. (2003) carried out a clinical and electrophysiologic study of 2 Italian families with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME). Both families showed linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2.
quotes: The authors report a clinical and electrophysiologic study of two Italian BAFME families showing linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2.

findings.statement: de Falco et al. (2003) noted that BAFME had been mapped to chromosome 8q24. Their finding that 2 Italian families were linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 supported genetic heterogeneity and the existence of non-Japanese families with BAFME.
quotes: Benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) has been mapped to chromosome 8q24; however, genetic heterogeneity has been recently suggested.
Their report supports the evidence of non-Japanese families with BAFME

findings.statement: de Falco et al. (2003) suggested that BAFME linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 might be allelic with the recently described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) syndrome.
quotes: suggests a possible allelism with the recently described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy syndrome

relevance_reason: Describes a European FAME family excluded from the 8q24 (FAME1) locus, which establishes genetic heterogeneity. This is the basis for a separate FAME locus.

findings.statement: Labauge et al. (2002) described a 4-generation European family with 18 members and familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME). Ten living and 3 deceased relatives were affected. In the 10 living patients, mean age at onset was 41 years (range, 30-60 years). Eight of the 13 affected individuals had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electrophysiologic studies in 5 patients confirmed the diagnosis of FAME.
quotes: A four-generation European kindred presenting with FAME, including 18 members, is described.
Ten living and three deceased relatives had the clinical characteristics of FAME. Mean age at onset of the 10 living patients was 41 years (range, 30-60 years).
Eight of the 13 affected subjects had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electrophysiologic studies confirmed the diagnosis of FAME in the five patients studied.

findings.statement: In the European family studied by Labauge et al. (2002), the pattern of inheritance was consistent with autosomal dominant transmission.
quotes: The pattern of inheritance was consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance.

findings.statement: Labauge et al. (2002) performed linkage analysis in the European FAME family using fluorescent microsatellites spanning the FAME/BAFME locus on 8q23.3-q24.1, and the locus was excluded. The authors concluded that this exclusion established genetic heterogeneity of the disorder. They also noted that the family extended the occurrence of FAME to non-Japanese patients.
quotes: Linkage analysis was performed with fluorescent microsatellites encompassing the FAME/BAFME locus (8q23.3-q24.1).
The locus responsible for FAME/BAFME was excluded.
Exclusion of linkage of this family to the locus for familial adult myoclonic epilepsy/benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy established the genetic heterogeneity of this disorder.

relevance_reason: This is the original description of ADCME (FAME2), including the clinical, neurophysiologic and linkage findings that map it to 2p11.1-q12.2.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree in which 8 individuals had a nonprogressive disorder with onset between 12 and 50 years of age. All of them had mainly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities.
quotes: We describe a pedigree in which eight individuals presented with a non-progressive disorder with onset between the ages of 12 and 50 years.
It was characterized by predominantly distal, semi-continuous rhythmic myoclonus (all patients), generalized tonic-clonic seizures (all patients) and complex partial seizures (three patients).
Most individuals had rarely suffered seizures and had a normal cognitive level, but three individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation.

phenotypes.text: frontotemporal and generalized interictal EEG abnormalities

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) found from neurophysiologic studies that the myoclonus was cortical in origin. In 5 patients, EEG over the contralateral rolandic area was coherent with EMG at 8 to 25 Hz, and EEG activity preceded EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms. Ipsilateral coherence in 2 patients was consistent with transcallosal spread. Patients had an enhanced C-reflex and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. Compared with controls, they also had a reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation and a shortened post-MEP silent period. The authors suggested that these findings reflect diffuse cortical hyperexcitability.
quotes: The frequency of coherence was 8-25 Hz and phase spectra confirmed that EEG activity preceded EMG activity by 8-15 ms.
The C-reflex at rest was enhanced and somatosensory and visual evoked potentials were of high amplitude.

These clinical and neuro- physiological characteristics suggest diffuse cortical hyperexcitability and high propensity for intra-hemispheric and inter-hemispheric cortical spread, as well as rhythmic myoclonic activity.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) found that inheritance in the ADCME family was autosomal dominant with high penetrance.
quotes: The pattern of inheritance was autosomal dominant with high penetrance.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) performed a genome-wide linkage analysis and identified a 12.4-cM critical region on 2p11.1-q12.2 between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897. The maximum 2-point lod score was 3.46 at theta = 0.0 for D2S2175, and the multipoint lod score reached 3.74 around D2S2175.
quotes: Genome-wide linkage analysis identified a critical region spanning 12.4 cM between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897 in 2p11.1-q12.2, with a maximum two-point LOD score of 3.46 at Theta 0.0 for marker D2S2175.
Multipoint LOD score values, reaching 3.74 around D2S2175, localize the ADCME gene to the centromeric region of chromosome 2.

findings.statement: Guerrini et al. (2001) excluded linkage to the familial adult myoclonic epilepsy locus on 8q23.3-q24 in their family. Based on the new chromosome 2 localization and the different phenotype, they defined ADCME as a new epilepsy syndrome.
quotes: The exclusion of the locus for familial adult myoclonic epilepsy on chromosome 8q23.3-q24 from linkage to our family and the new localization of the responsible gene to chromosome 2cen, together with the different phenotype, define a new epilepsy syndrome.
